title: Precedent, Statute, and the Limits of Interpretation
text:
Common law reasoning rests on the doctrine of stare decisis, which obliges courts to follow precedents established by higher tribunals in analogous cases. Yet the doctrine is not mechanical, for judges must determine which features of an earlier decision were material to its outcome and which were incidental. This distinction between the ratio decidendi and the obiter dicta is often contested, since advocates seek to frame precedents narrowly or broadly according to their clients' interests.

Textualist critics argue that statutes must be interpreted according to their ordinary meaning at enactment, lest judges substitute their own policy preferences for the will of the legislature. Purposivists reply that rigid literalism can defeat the very aims a statute was designed to achieve, and that a court faithful to legislative intent must sometimes look beyond the words. Neither camp has fully vindicated its claim, which is why appellate judgments so often read as a negotiation between competing theories of legitimacy.

questions.text: According to the passage, what does stare decisis oblige courts to do?
options: Follow precedents established by higher tribunals in analogous cases
Ignore all earlier decisions in favour of statutes
Apply the literal words of every contract
Decide each case without reference to the past

questions.text: What do purposivists argue about rigid literalism?
options: It always produces the most just outcome
It can defeat the aims a statute was designed to achieve
It is the only method consistent with legislative intent
It was abandoned by all courts in the twentieth century

questions.text: What can be inferred about how advocates treat precedents?
options: They treat precedents as fixed and identical in every case
They shape how precedents are described to suit their clients' needs
They avoid precedents whenever a statute exists
They regard the ratio decidendi as irrelevant

questions.text: What does the passage suggest about appellate judgments?
options: They are determined entirely by the words of statutes
They reflect a contest between rival theories of legitimacy
They have been resolved in favour of the textualist position
They rarely involve questions of interpretation

vocabulary.definition: earlier decisions that guide how similar cases are judged
similar in important respects, so comparable
secondary or minor, not central to a result
disputed or challenged by different people

paragraph_translations: O raciocínio do common law repousa sobre a doutrina do stare decisis, que obriga os tribunais a seguir os precedentes estabelecidos por instâncias superiores em casos análogos. Contudo, a doutrina não é mecânica, pois os juízes devem determinar quais aspectos de uma decisão anterior foram relevantes para o resultado e quais foram incidentais. Essa distinção entre a ratio decidendi e o obiter dictum é frequentemente contestada, já que os advogados buscam formular os precedentes de modo restrito ou amplo conforme os interesses de seus clientes.

Os críticos textualistas argumentam que as leis devem ser interpretadas segundo seu sentido ordinário no momento da promulgação, para que os juízes não substituam suas próprias preferências de política pela vontade do legislativo. Os defensores da interpretação teleológica respondem que o literalismo rígido pode frustrar os próprios objetivos para os quais a lei foi criada, e que um tribunal fiel à intenção legislativa deve, por vezes, olhar além das palavras. Nenhum dos lados logrou plenamente sustentar sua tese, razão pela qual os julgamentos de instâncias superiores tantas vezes se assemelham a uma negociação entre teorias concorrentes de legitimidade.
